Neonatal Lowland copperheads (Austrelaps superbus) emerge from their parchment-shelled eggs after a period of intra-ovarian development, with parturition producing live young that average a snout-vent length of 17.5 centimeters [Lb = 17.5 centimeters]. This modest size at birth, coupled with a corresponding birth weight of just 3.4 grams [Wwb = 3.4 grams], reflects the energetic constraints of gestation in a temperate-zone elapid. The neonates are immediately capable of independent locomotion and prey capture, a typical pattern for viperoid snakes. Field studies in the highland regions of southeastern Australia indicate that these hatchlings grow rapidly during their first active season, feeding primarily on small skinks and frogs. The initial mass, while slight, provides sufficient endogenous yolk reserves to sustain the young during the first few days of exogenous feeding transition. Comparative data from related Australasian elapids suggest that the size at birth in Austrelaps superbus is intermediate, falling below that of large-bodied genera like Pseudechis but exceeding that of smaller fossorial species. This size likely reflects a trade-off between maternal brood size and offspring viability in a cool, seasonal environment where growing seasons are short.

Sexual maturation in male Lowland copperheads occurs upon reaching a snout-vent length of 50 centimeters [Lp = 50 centimeters], a threshold that signals the onset of pubertal development and the capacity for spermatogenesis. Females, by contrast, do not initiate gonadal maturation until they attain a more substantial body size, with puberty documented at a snout-vent length of 60 centimeters [Lp = 60 centimeters]. This sexual dimorphism in maturation size is consistent with the pattern observed across many elapids, wherein the larger sex delays reproductive investment to accrue the somatic capital necessary for gestation. Males typically reach this size within two to three years post-hatching under favorable thermal conditions, whereas females require a longer growth period given their higher size threshold. The attainment of these pubertal lengths marks a critical life-history transition, after which individuals can divert resources toward gamete production rather than exclusively toward somatic growth. Field recapture data indicate that once males surpass the 50-centimeter milestone, they begin actively searching for receptive females during the austral spring breeding season, engaging in combat with rival males.

Female Lowland copperheads ultimately attain a maximum recorded snout-vent length of 97 centimeters [Li = 97 centimeters], representing the asymptotic body size for this sex under optimal growing conditions. Males achieve an even larger ultimate size, reaching a snout-vent length of 110 centimeters [Li = 110 centimeters], a difference that is reflected in their heavier build and longer average lifespan. This pronounced sexual size dimorphism is uncommon among elapids but is well-documented in this species, likely driven by sexual selection for male contest competition. The ultimate body weight for females is considerable, with gravid individuals reaching an adult body mass of up to 432 grams [Wwi = up to 432 grams], a value that underscores the substantial energy reserves required to produce a large litter of live young. This mass was derived from morphometric data, scaling from a known female of 71.77 centimeters SVL that weighed 174.9 grams. The relationship between length and mass in this species follows a cubic function, consistent with isometric growth in body volume. These large-bodied females are capable of producing litters of between 10 and 20 neonates, depending on maternal condition.

Reproductive output in the Lowland copperhead is tightly linked to female body size, with larger individuals achieving higher fecundity. At a snout-vent length of 136.7 centimeters, an exceptionally large female, nearly at the upper size limit recorded for the species, produces approximately 11.9 offspring per year [Ri = approximately 11.9 offspring per year] under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a constant temperature of 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C]. This high reproductive potential is rarely realized in the wild, where cooler temperatures and resource limitation reduce annual output. Biennial reproduction is common in many populations, with females skipping years between litters to rebuild fat stores. The observed rate at this size class provides an upper benchmark for the species' intrinsic capacity. Captive breeding studies confirm that when provided with ad libitum food and optimal thermal regimes, females can sustain such output over several consecutive years. The temperature dependence of this rate is critical, as gestation and embryonic development are highly sensitive to thermal variation, with prolonged cool spells potentially interrupting development.

Maximum lifespan in the Lowland copperhead has been documented at 10 years [am = 10 years] in a captive setting where individuals were maintained at a constant temperature of 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C], a thermal regime that approximates the upper end of the species' preferred active body temperature range. In wild populations, longevity is likely shorter due to predation, disease, and seasonal resource bottlenecks. Radiotelemetry studies in the Victorian highlands have tracked individuals for up to seven active seasons, suggesting that few animals survive into their eighth or ninth year. The captive maximum of 3,650 days [am = 3,650 days] represents the upper physiological limit under ideal conditions, with senescence typically becoming apparent in the final year through reduced feeding rates and lower locomotor performance at a temperature of 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C]. This lifespan is modest compared to some large pythons and boas but is typical for elapids of this body size. The relatively short life expectancy, combined with delayed female maturation and moderate litter sizes, suggests that population persistence depends heavily on adult survivorship during the reproductive years.
